strengths: The paper offers a clear and useful unifying view of several diffusion concept-erasure losses as f-divergence objectives, with both closed-form Gaussian cases and a variational formulation. Connecting Concept Ablation/DoCo-like objectives to this framework is a meaningful conceptual contribution.

The gradient analysis for closed-form KL/MSE, Hellinger, and chi-square losses is intuitive and helps explain different erasure/preservation trade-offs. The empirical gradient plots and qualitative examples support the claim that Hellinger can be less prone to destructive updates.

The experiments cover several anchor choices, several concepts, different iteration budgets, and both single-concept and sequential erasure settings. The appendices provide many quantitative tables rather than relying only on cherry-picked images.
The writing is generally readable, and the paper makes a reasonable effort to situate itself relative to concept erasure, post-processing, closed-form editing, and adversarial unlearning methods.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence is not strong enough for the broad claim that f-divergence methods, especially Hellinger, consistently outperform MSE. In several tables MSE has comparable or better target erasure, while Hellinger mainly trades weaker erasure for better preservation; the paper often presents this as superiority rather than a nuanced trade-off.

The evaluation is narrow for a main-track diffusion unlearning paper: SD v1.4 only, a small set of six concepts, limited comparison mainly to MSE/Concept Ablation, and no strong baselines such as ESD variants, UCE/RECE/MACE, recent robust erasure methods, or DoCo despite being discussed as related.

The unlearning assessment relies heavily on CLIP score/accuracy and KID between pre/post generations. These are weak proxies for actual concept removal, copyright/style erasure, prompt robustness, and safety. There is no adversarial prompt evaluation, no retention set beyond selected concepts, no human evaluation, and no measurement of relearning or robustness to fine-tuning despite these being important in the motivation.

The theory is useful but limited. The closed-form objectives largely reduce to monotone transformations of the same Gaussian mean-matching distance under equal-variance assumptions, so the main difference is optimization dynamics rather than a fundamentally different optimum. The local convergence result for the variational formulation depends on strong equilibrium/full-rank assumptions and does not establish global behavior or practical convergence for the implemented neural objectives.

The variational formulation is underspecified and empirically weak. The paper claims applicability to any f-divergence, but the experiments suggest the variational methods can be artifact-prone and sometimes fail to erase effectively; implementation details for the discriminator/objective are insufficient for assessing or reproducing these results.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper gives hardware, batch size, some sampler details, concepts, and iteration counts, but omits important hyperparameters such as optimizer settings, learning rates, trainable modules, exact prompts/sample counts, random seeds, model checkpoints after unlearning, and code availability.

The presentation has issues that make some evidence hard to interpret: large tables are dense, several claims rely on qualitative figures, KID interpretation for erased concepts changes depending on the intended replacement behavior, and statistical uncertainty is absent.

Limitations and ethics are underdeveloped. The introduction motivates NSFW content, copyrighted styles, and personal information, but the experiments do not evaluate NSFW removal, privacy leakage, copyright memorization, misuse risks, or failure modes of releasing partially erased models. There is no explicit limitations section.

strengths: The paper identifies a real and relevant problem: concept unlearning for text-to-image diffusion models, with a useful framing of common MSE-based anchor matching as a special case of divergence minimization.

The closed-form derivations for several divergences and the observation that Hellinger and chi-square induce different gradient scalings are mathematically intuitive and could be useful as a design lens for unlearning losses.

The manuscript includes both closed-form and variational variants, evaluates several anchor choices, and reports results over multiple target concepts including objects/characters and artistic styles.
The appendix contains a reasonable amount of additional experimental detail and tables, including training-step ablations and regularization variants.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim that f-divergences consistently outperform MSE is not convincingly supported. Many reported results show mixed trade-offs: MSE often erases as well or better on CS/CA, Hellinger sometimes preserves better KID but also weakens erasure, and variational methods are explicitly described as artifact-prone. The evidence supports, at most, a tuning trade-off rather than clear superiority.

The technical novelty is limited for the closed-form part. Under the paper's equal-variance Gaussian assumption, the alternative closed-form f-divergence objectives reduce to monotone transformations or gradient reweightings of the same MSE distance, with the same optimum. The gradient analysis is largely a direct consequence of this reweighting, so the theoretical contribution feels modest relative to the framing.

The variational framework is under-validated and somewhat unclear. It is claimed to support any f-divergence, but the experiments cover only a few cases, the discriminator/critic setup is not sufficiently specified, and the appendix notation appears inconsistent about whether the second expectation evaluates T on Phi or the unlearned model. The local convergence theorem relies on strong local, continuous-time, full-rank assumptions and does not establish stable or useful behavior in the actual finite-step neural optimization setting.

The evaluation is too narrow for an ICML main-track unlearning paper. It uses Stable Diffusion v1.4 and only a small set of six concepts; it does not evaluate standard safety/copyright unlearning benchmarks, adversarial prompts, prompt paraphrases, relearning/finetuning robustness, or broad collateral damage across large prompt suites.

Baselines are insufficient. The paper discusses ESD, UCE, RECE, MACE, and other recent erasure methods, but the main empirical comparison is primarily against MSE and Concept Ablation. Without competitive modern baselines, the significance of the proposed framework is hard to judge.

Metrics are weak and sometimes confusing. CLIP score and CLIP accuracy are indirect proxies for erasure, KID is computed against the original model rather than a target distribution and is interpreted differently depending on the goal, and no uncertainty estimates, seeds, or statistical tests are provided. Negative KID values are reported without enough care, making several quantitative comparisons hard to trust.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper gives hardware, batch size, concepts, sampler steps, and some iteration counts, but omits important details such as learning rates, optimizer settings, trainable parameter subsets, exact prompt lists/counts, random seeds, code availability, discriminator architecture for variational methods, and implementation details for regularization.

Presentation is uneven. Several tables are extremely dense and difficult to read, key results are pushed to the appendix, qualitative claims are stronger than the quantitative evidence, and there are typographical/formatting issues such as missing spaces, awkward wording, and ambiguous notation.

Limitations and ethics are not adequately treated. The paper motivates unlearning via NSFW, copyright, and privacy concerns, but does not discuss failure modes, misuse, false assurance, evaluation gaps, or the ethical risk of claiming removal from a model based only on weak prompt-level proxies.

strengths: The paper proposes a clean and useful unifying view of diffusion-model concept unlearning through f-divergences, showing how standard MSE/KL-style objectives arise as a special case and how alternatives such as Hellinger and Pearson chi-square lead to different optimization behavior.

The closed-form Hellinger objective is practically attractive: it preserves the same simple fine-tuning structure as MSE while providing bounded gradients, and the manuscript connects this property to improved preservation and fewer visual artifacts.

The theoretical analysis is relevant and reasonably well motivated, with both gradient comparisons for closed-form losses and local convergence analysis for the variational min-max formulation. The discussion of convergence speed as a function of f''(1) gives useful guidance rather than only a new loss recipe.

The empirical section covers several concept types, including fictional objects/characters and artistic styles, multiple anchor choices, closed-form versus variational objectives, single-concept erasure, and a sequential multi-concept setting. The results generally support the claim that Hellinger can offer a better erasure-preservation tradeoff than plain MSE/Concept Ablation in the tested settings.
The paper is mostly readable and well organized, with appendices that include derivations, additional related work, implementation details, and extended tables.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence is still narrower than the main claims suggest. All experiments appear to use Stable Diffusion v1.4 and a small set of six primary concepts; there is no evaluation on newer T2I backbones, broader prompt distributions, adversarial prompt attacks, real copyrighted/NSFW removal benchmarks, or post-unlearning re-learning robustness.

Baselines are limited for a current ICML unlearning paper. The manuscript discusses methods such as ESD, UCE, MACE, RECELER, and others, but the main quantitative comparisons are largely against MSE/Concept Ablation-style objectives rather than a broad set of strong recent unlearning methods.

The evaluation relies heavily on CLIP Score, CLIP Accuracy, KID, and qualitative examples. These metrics are imperfect proxies for successful unlearning, preservation, and image quality; there is no human study, safety classifier evaluation, memorization/privacy test, or analysis of false erasure versus genuine removal.

The theory is useful but local and assumption-heavy. The convergence result concerns an idealized continuous-time min-max system near equilibrium and depends on assumptions such as existence of an equilibrium and sufficient model/discriminator behavior; it does not by itself establish global convergence or practical unlearning reliability.

The claimed consistent superiority over MSE is somewhat overstated. Some tables show tradeoffs where Hellinger preserves better but erases less aggressively, or where regularization weakens erasure substantially. The variational methods are also described as more aggressive but often produce artifacts and are not clearly superior quantitatively.

Reproducibility is only partial. The paper reports hardware, batch size, sampler steps, concepts, and some training details, but I did not see a code release, random seeds, full prompt lists, optimizer settings, learning rates, or variance over multiple runs. The dense tables also make it hard to audit exact comparisons.

The manuscript lacks an explicit limitations and ethics section. This is especially important because concept unlearning in T2I models directly concerns copyrighted content, NSFW content, privacy, dual-use censorship/removal, and potential over-erasure of benign concepts.

Presentation is occasionally rough: several tables are very difficult to read, some extracted formatting suggests cramped or ambiguous notation, and the main text sometimes makes strong claims from qualitative examples without enough statistical support.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem in text-to-image diffusion model unlearning and gives a clean unifying view of many MSE/KL-style concept-erasure objectives through f-divergences.

The closed-form derivations for Gaussian denoising distributions are useful: they show that Hellinger and Pearson chi-square variants amount to different per-sample gradient scalings of the familiar MSE objective, which is a simple and practically relevant insight.

The empirical evaluation is fairly broad, covering style erasure, object erasure, sequential multi-concept erasure, nudity erasure, adversarial prompts, and several model families including SD 1.4/1.5/2.1/XL plus appendix experiments on diffusion-transformer-style models.

The Hellinger closed-form method is consistently plausible as a useful default: the reported results often show better preservation of non-target concepts and lower KID than MSE while maintaining comparable or better erasure.

The paper includes meaningful ablations/comparisons between closed-form and variational objectives, multiple f-divergences, anchor choices, regularization variants, and iteration counts, which helps clarify when aggressive erasure harms fidelity.

The presentation of the main framework is mostly clear, and the theoretical gradient analysis gives an intuitive explanation for the observed stability differences between Hellinger, MSE/KL, and chi-square losses.
weaknesses: The originality is moderate. The main practical contribution is largely a theoretically motivated reweighting of existing MSE-based diffusion unlearning losses; the framework is elegant, but many ingredients follow directly from known f-divergence identities and prior concept-ablation formulations.

Some central claims are stronger than the evidence supports. The paper repeatedly suggests consistent superiority of H-DMU, but results show trade-offs across CS, CA, KID, anchor choice, training length, and target concept; in some tables the improvements over tuned CAbl/MSE are small or mixed.

The theoretical convergence analysis for the variational formulation relies on strong local assumptions: existence of an exact equilibrium matching the target and anchor conditional distributions, full-rank conditions, infinitesimal learning-rate dynamics, and an ideal discriminator setting. This makes the analysis mainly qualitative rather than a strong guarantee for the actual diffusion fine-tuning procedure.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The abstract says code is available but the link appears blank, and while many hyperparameters are listed, the paper does not provide enough detail on prompts, seeds, prompt counts per experiment, exact model checkpoints, classifier settings, or variance over runs to fully reproduce the reported numbers.

The experimental reporting lacks uncertainty estimates. The appendix states that main experiments average over multiple random seeds, but tables generally omit standard deviations or confidence intervals, which is important for CLIP-based metrics and small prompt sets.

Baseline fairness is somewhat hard to judge. The paper says CAbl hyperparameters were optimized for nudity and matched to H-DMU/P-DMU, but it is less clear whether all state-of-the-art baselines were equally tuned under comparable budgets, prompts, and regularization choices.

The evaluation relies heavily on CLIP score/accuracy and KID between pre- and post-erasure generations. These metrics are useful proxies but imperfect for concept unlearning, especially for artistic style and NSFW content; more human evaluation or stronger semantic/identity leakage tests would strengthen the claims.

The variational part is less convincing than the closed-form part. The min-max formulation is presented as general, but empirically it is noisy, often less stable, and not clearly competitive except as an aggressive erasure mode; this reduces the practical significance of the fully general f-divergence claim.

The limitations and ethics treatment are weak. The impact statement says no societal consequences need highlighting, despite the paper directly handling nudity suppression, copyrighted/artistic styles, adversarial prompt robustness, and model modification for content control. This deserves a concrete discussion of misuse, over-removal, censorship, artist consent, evaluation bias, and release safeguards.

Presentation is generally readable but dense, with key experimental protocol details pushed to the appendix and some overclaiming in the narrative. The paper would benefit from a clearer limitations section and a more calibrated statement of what is actually proven versus empirically observed.

strengths: The paper identifies a clean connection between common MSE-based diffusion concept erasure objectives and KL divergence, then formulates a broader f-divergence view. This is a useful organizing lens for existing and future objectives.
The closed-form Hellinger and chi-square variants are simple to implement and computationally comparable to MSE, which makes the main practical proposal accessible.

The manuscript includes a broad empirical sweep across style erasure, object erasure, nudity erasure, adversarial prompts, multi-concept erasure, and several Stable Diffusion variants. The nudity results for H-DMU are especially promising relative to CAbl and several baselines.

The authors discuss the trade-off between aggressive erasure and preservation, and the gradient-scaling analysis gives some intuition for why bounded Hellinger-like objectives may preserve non-target behavior better than chi-square-like objectives.
weaknesses: The central novelty is modest. For the closed-form methods, H-DMU and chi-square-DMU are essentially monotone transformations of the same denoiser MSE with different per-sample gradient weights. The paper overstates this as a unified unlearning framework without adequately comparing to simpler robust-loss or sample-reweighting baselines that could produce similar behavior.

The theoretical contribution is weaker than presented. The f-divergence objective does not generally inherit the KL trajectory decomposition used in prior work, and the convergence analysis is local, assumption-heavy, and mainly concerns the variational min-max formulation, while the paper ultimately recommends the closed-form Hellinger method. This limits how much the theory supports the main empirical claims.

The empirical evidence is not convincing enough for the breadth of the claims. The paper reports many tables but gives no clear uncertainty estimates, exact number of seeds, or significance testing. Several claims of consistent dominance rely on small metric differences, aggregate preserved-concept scores, and qualitative examples.

The evaluation metrics are fragile for the stated goals. CLIP Score/CLIP Accuracy are weak proxies for actual concept removal, KID is computed between original and edited model generations rather than against real data, and negative KID values appear without sufficient explanation. For NSFW erasure, detector choice and failure modes are not discussed in enough detail.

Baseline fairness is hard to assess. Some comparisons use the authors' reimplementations, some appear to use shared prompts, and hyperparameter tuning for baselines versus f-DMU is not fully specified. The paper needs clearer accounting of training steps, learning-rate tuning, prompt sets, image counts, and whether each baseline was run under matched compute.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The abstract says code is available but the link is blank in the manuscript, and important details such as prompt lists, random seeds, discriminator architecture for variational methods, and full hyperparameter search procedures are missing or underspecified.

The variational framework is advertised as allowing any f-divergence, but the experiments themselves show it can be noisy and quality-degrading with diffusion fine-tuning batch sizes. This makes the broad framework claim less practically compelling.

The limitations and ethics treatment are inadequate. The impact statement says no societal consequences need highlighting despite the paper targeting NSFW removal and copyrighted artistic styles, both of which have clear safety, misuse, and creator-rights implications.

strengths: The paper gives a clean and useful generalization of common diffusion-model concept unlearning losses: it shows that the usual MSE objective corresponds to a KL instance and develops an f-divergence framework with both closed-form Gaussian losses and a variational min-max formulation.

The closed-form Hellinger and chi-square instances are technically appealing because they are simple MSE-like objectives with different per-sample gradient scaling, and the paper connects these gradient properties to observed unlearning dynamics.

The empirical evaluation is broad for this area: artistic style, object, sequential multi-concept erasure, nudity erasure, adversarial prompts, multiple Stable Diffusion versions, SDXL, and some DiT/flow-based models are considered.

The results are generally convincing that closed-form Hellinger improves the erasure/preservation trade-off over the MSE/CAbl-style baseline in many settings, especially for prior preservation and nudity erasure on SD 1.5.
The paper is well organized and the appendices provide many derivations, implementation details, and additional tables, making the core method relatively easy to reproduce in principle.
weaknesses: Some claims are stronger than the evidence supports. For example, H-DMU is described as outperforming state-of-the-art methods on adversarial nudity prompts, but CAbl is better on Ring-A-Bell in Table 4/Table 10, and SD3 results are marginal or mixed.

The theoretical analysis is useful but limited: the variational convergence result is local, assumption-dependent, and does not fully explain finite-batch discriminator behavior in practical diffusion fine-tuning, which the experiments themselves identify as problematic.

The evaluation relies heavily on CLIP Score, CLIP Accuracy, and KID. These are reasonable proxies, but concept erasure and preservation would benefit from more robust human or external classifier evaluation, uncertainty intervals, and clearer reporting of the number of random seeds.

Reproducibility is not fully satisfactory as written: the abstract says code is available but the link appears blank, and several important choices such as prompt sets, exact seed counts, and checkpoint selection criteria are only partially specified or deferred to prior repositories.

The ethics/impact discussion is too thin for a paper on erasing nudity, copyrighted styles, and unsafe content from generative models. It warns about offensive outputs but does not meaningfully discuss misuse, overblocking, false confidence in unlearning, or evaluation limitations for safety-sensitive deployment.

The variational framework is presented as a major part of the unified contribution, but empirically it often performs worse or is unstable due to coarse divergence estimates; this reduces the practical impact of the most general part of the method.
